analysis.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject, and אֹתָם identifies the humans as recipients. God then addresses them directly with פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ, “be fruitful and multiply,” expressing the fruitfulness included in the blessing.
analysis.morphology: Piel wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־ and no suffix
analysis.sense: to bless living creatures with fruitfulness

draft.change: Add Genesis 1:28 to the evidence for the existing object-pronoun sense in et.
draft.definition: With a pronominal suffix, אֵת expresses the direct object separately from the verb.
draft.evidence: Genesis 1:28 uses אֹתָם as the direct object of וַיְבָרֶךְ, “he blessed them.”

analysis.evidence: In וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם אֱלֹהִים, God is the subject and אֹתָם identifies the people he blessed. The following וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם refers to the same people as those to whom God spoke.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object marker in its suffixed form אֹת־ with the third-person masculine plural pronominal suffix ־ָם.
analysis.sense: Carries a pronominal suffix as the direct object of a verb.

analysis.evidence: In וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם אֱלֹהִים, “God blessed them,” אֱלֹהִים is the subject of the third-person masculine singular verb וַיְבָרֶךְ. The singular agreement identifies God as the one who blesses them.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine plural absolute, with singular verbal agreement.

analysis.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject, and לָהֶם identifies the addressees. The plural imperatives פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ (“be fruitful and multiply”) begin God's direct speech.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־ and no suffix

analysis.evidence: In וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם אֱלֹהִים (“God said to them”), אֱלֹהִים is the subject of the singular verb וַיֹּאמֶר. The speaker is the same God who has just blessed them.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute noun with singular reference and agreement.

analysis.evidence: God addresses the humans with the plural command פְּרוּ. The following commands וּרְבוּ (“and multiply”) and וּמִלְאוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ (“and fill the earth”) show that fruitfulness here means producing offspring.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperative, second person masculine plural

analysis.evidence: God pairs וּרְבוּ with פְּרוּ ‘be fruitful’ and then commands the addressees to fill the earth. The sequence identifies the increase as growth in the human population through offspring.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ ‘and’ + Qal imperative, second person masculine plural.

analysis.evidence: אֶת marks הָאָרֶץ, “the earth,” as the direct object of וּמִלְאוּ. Following “be fruitful and multiply,” the command tells the addressees to fill the earth with their descendants.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperative, second person masculine plural, prefixed with the conjunction וּ.

analysis.evidence: In וּמִלְאוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ, “and fill the earth,” אֶת marks הָאָרֶץ (“the earth”) as the definite direct object of the imperative וּמִלְאוּ (“and fill”).
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle in the form אֶת, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וּמִלְאוּ אֶת הָאָרֶץ, the earth is what humanity is commanded to fill. The feminine singular suffix in וְכִבְשֻׁהָ refers back to it: “and subdue it.”
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ + common noun, singular absolute, feminine here.

draft.change: Add a root article for כבש with the Qal sense ‘subdue’.
draft.definition: To subdue land is to bring it under one’s control.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 1:28 the earth is the object of both filling and subduing. The following command to rule over its creatures supports the sense of gaining mastery.

analysis.evidence: The suffix הָ refers back to הָאָרֶץ ‘the earth’ in the command ‘fill the earth’. The same people are commanded to subdue it. The next imperative, וּרְדוּ ‘and rule’, takes the living creatures as its objects.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ ‘and’ + Qal imperative, second masculine plural + third feminine singular direct-object suffix הָ ‘it’.
analysis.sense: Bring the earth under human control.

analysis.evidence: וּרְדוּ continues the plural commands addressed to the humans. The following phrases with בְּ identify the creatures they are to rule over: the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and every living creature that moves on the earth.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperative, second person masculine plural, with conjunction וּ־

analysis.evidence: In וּרְדוּ בִּדְגַת הַיָּם, “rule over the fish of the sea,” the verb וּרְדוּ governs בְּ, and הַיָּם completes the construct phrase. The parallel phrase וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, “and over the birds of the heavens,” supports the collective reading.
analysis.morphology: Prefixed preposition בְּ (here בִּ) + feminine singular construct noun דְגַת, used collectively.

analysis.evidence: In בִּדְגַת הַיָּם, “over the fish of the sea,” הַיָּם completes the construct phrase and identifies the fishes’ habitat. The parallel phrases place birds in the heavens and land creatures on the earth.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ + masculine singular absolute common noun.

analysis.evidence: וּרְדוּ governs the preposition בְּ. The phrase וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם means “and over the birds of the heavens” and parallels בִּדְגַת הַיָּם, “over the fish of the sea.”
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ and preposition בְּ prefixed to a masculine singular construct noun used collectively.

analysis.evidence: In וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, “the birds of the sky,” the sky identifies the birds’ domain, alongside the sea for fish and the land for creeping creatures.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine plural noun in the absolute state.

analysis.evidence: In וּבְכָל חַיָּה הָרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל הָאָרֶץ, כָל quantifies the singular חַיָּה, ‘every living creature that moves on the earth.’ The prefixed בְּ־ marks what the addressees are to rule over, as it does in the preceding phrases for the fish and the birds.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ־ ‘and’ + preposition בְּ־ ‘over’ + masculine singular construct noun כָל.

analysis.evidence: In וּבְכָל חַיָּה הָרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל הָאָרֶץ, כָל gives the scope “every,” and the feminine singular participle הָרֹמֶשֶׂת agrees with חַיָּה. The phrase denotes every creature that moves on the earth, alongside the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular absolute noun, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: הָרֹמֶשֶׂת agrees in gender and number with חַיָּה, “living creature.” The phrase עַל הָאָרֶץ specifies where it moves, yielding “every living creature that moves about on the earth.”
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ + Qal active participle, feminine singular absolute.

analysis.evidence: In הָרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל הָאָרֶץ, “that moves on the earth,” עַל introduces the surface on which the creature moves.
analysis.morphology: Preposition without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In הָרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל הָאָרֶץ, עַל marks the ground as the surface on which the creature moves.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, singular absolute, with the definite article הָ־.
